Average annual energy savings by insulation level for attic floor insulation upgrade compared to baseline Figure 12 shows that across the 235,950 applicable units, older homes generally consume more energy than newer construction. For instance, the average baseline energy use is 33,415 kWh/unit/year for pre-1940s units, followed by 30,386 kWh for 1940s units, and 22,446 kWh for 1970s units. In contrast, homes built in the 1980s or later tend to have lower energy use: ranging from 20,970 kWh for 1990s units to 19,024 kWh for 2010s units. There are a few exceptions to this general pattern. For example, some 1950s homes show slightly higher baseline consumption than 1940s units, likely due to variations in floor area, occupant behavior, or HVAC system efficiency. Despite these variations, older homes consistently benefit most from attic floor insulation upgrades, as described below. 18 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 12. Annual energy consumption by vintage for baseline and attic floor insulation upgrade As shown in Figure 13, upgrading attic floor insulation to R-60 (climate zones 2–8) or R-49 (zone 1) results in greater energy savings for older homes. For example, pre-1940s homes save an average of 885 kWh/unit/year, and 1940s units save 973 kWh. In contrast, 1990s and 2000s homes save only 306 kWh and 289 kWh, respectively. Figure 14 shows a similar trend in percent savings: 2.6% for 1940s homes versus just above 1.4% for homes built in the 1990s and after. These patterns are largely due to lower baseline insulation levels in older homes, which often have R-values below R-19 or are uninsulated. In comparison, newer homes typically start at R- 30 or higher, limiting the potential for improvement (Figure 1). 19 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
